subject: anatomy
title: Portosystemic Anastomoses: Varices, Caput Medusae, and Hepatic Veins

steps.tx: Portosystemic anastomoses (portocaval communications) are microscopic collateral channels linking the portal venous system with the systemic venous circulation. In physiological health, blood flow through these embryonic shunts is negligible; however, portal hypertension reverses flow, dilating these thin-walled channels into prominent **varices**.
steps.say: Portosystemic anastomoses are embryonic collaterals linking portal and systemic veins. While negligible in health, portal hypertension forces blood backward through them, dilating them into varices.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic illustrating portosystemic collateral sites: gastro-oesophageal, rectal, and umbilical
vis.caption: Primary anatomical sites of portosystemic collaterals dilated in portal hypertension. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The most clinically significant portosystemic communication occurs at the lower end of the oesophagus. Here, the oesophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein (portal) anastomose with the oesophageal veins draining into the azygos and hemiazygos veins (systemic), producing fragile submucosal **oesophageal varices**.
steps.say: The most dangerous communication lies at the lower oesophagus, where left gastric tributaries join azygos veins. In portal hypertension, these submucosal veins form bleeding oesophageal varices.

left.title: Portal Inflow Component
points: Oesophageal branches of left gastric vein
Direct tributary of portal vein
Transmits high retrogradely elevated pressure
Lacks venous valves to restrict reflux

right.title: Systemic Inflow Component
points: Oesophageal tributaries of azygos vein
Drains into superior vena cava
Thin submucosal veins in distal 5 cm
Prone to rupture from mechanical food bolus abrasion

steps.tx: The most clinically significant portosystemic communication is at the lower oesophagus, where left gastric tributaries carrying portal blood meet veins draining to the azygos and hemiazygos systems. Those submucosal channels become fragile **oesophageal varices** once portal pressure rises. Terlipressin narrows splanchnic arterioles, cuts blood entering the portal vein, and thereby lowers inflow and pressure in the bleeding varix while endoscopy is prepared.
steps.say: Left gastric tributaries join azygos veins at the lower oesophagus, and portal hypertension balloons them into bleeding submucosal varices. Terlipressin squeezes splanchnic arterioles so less blood flows into the portal system. Pressure in the varix falls and bleeding eases while endoscopy is set up.

vis.alt: Terlipressin constricting splanchnic arterioles so less portal blood reaches bleeding oesophageal varices.
vis.caption: Splanchnic vessels narrow under terlipressin, portal inflow falls, and pressure drops in submucosal varices at the lower oesophagus. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Rupture of dilated oesophageal varices produces sudden, exsanguinating hematemesis, carrying a thirty percent mortality rate per bleeding episode. Emergency endoscopic intervention utilizes endoscopic band ligation to arrest hemorrhage, alongside intravenous infusions of **terlipressin** or octreotide to induce splanchnic vasoconstriction and lower portal inflow.
steps.say: Ruptured oesophageal varices cause life-threatening hematemesis. Emergency therapy combines endoscopic band ligation with intravenous terlipressin or octreotide to lower splanchnic blood flow.

vis.alt: Terlipressin splanchnic vasoconstriction reducing portal inflow and variceal bleeding in portal hypertension
vis.caption: Terlipressin splanchnic vasoconstriction reducing portal inflow and variceal bleeding in portal hypertension. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The second major portosystemic anastomosis is located in the anal canal. The superior rectal vein (portal, continuing as inferior mesenteric) anastomoses with the middle and **inferior rectal veins** (systemic, draining via internal iliac and internal pudendal veins into the IVC), producing internal hemorrhoidal engorgement.
steps.say: A second major anastomosis sits in the anal canal, where the superior rectal vein meets middle and inferior rectal veins. Engorgement contributes to bleeding rectal varices and hemorrhoids.

steps.tx: At the umbilicus, paraumbilical veins running in the falciform ligament connect the left branch of the portal vein with the superficial epigastric veins. Severe portal hypertension recanalizes these veins, directing blood radially into the systemic veins of the abdominal wall to create the clinical sign termed **caput medusae**.
steps.say: At the umbilicus, paraumbilical veins connect the portal vein to abdominal wall veins. In portal hypertension, recanalization produces caput medusae radiating out from the navel.

left.title: Caput Medusae Flow Pattern
points: Direction of flow radiates away from umbilicus
Flow directed upward above umbilicus (to SVC)
Flow directed downward below umbilicus (to IVC)
Diagnostic of portal hypertension

right.title: Inferior Vena Cava Obstruction
points: Direction of flow is entirely upward toward the head
Flow ascends from below umbilicus past chest wall
Shunts lower body blood to superior vena cava
Diagnostic of IVC occlusion or thrombosis

steps.tx: In the retroperitoneal gutters, the **veins of Retzius** form microscopic shunts connecting retroperitoneal colonic and duodenal mesenteric veins (portal) with retroperitoneal parietal, lumbar, and renal systemic veins. During retroperitoneal surgery in cirrhotic patients, dividing these engorged shunts provokes diffuse, uncontrollable venous hemorrhage.
steps.say: The veins of Retzius connect colonic mesenteric veins with lumbar systemic veins in the retroperitoneum. In cirrhotic patients, cutting these engorged shunts causes heavy venous bleeding.

nodes.label: Sinusoidal Fibrosis Increases Splanchnic Mesenteric Outflow Resistance
Retrograde Flow Dilates Retroperitoneal Veins of Retzius
Collaterals Empty Directly into Lumbar and Parietal Veins
Severe Diffuse Bleeding during Retroperitoneal Organ Mobilization

steps.tx: Refractory variceal bleeding can be treated by creating an artificial portosystemic shunt. Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (**TIPS**) places an expandable metallic stent between a hepatic vein branch (systemic) and an intrahepatic portal vein branch under fluoroscopic guidance, decompressing portal pressure without open surgery.
steps.say: Refractory variceal bleeding is treated with a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS). A stent is placed between a hepatic vein and portal branch, decompressing the portal system.

left.title: TIPS Procedure Benefits
points: Minimally invasive endovascular route via internal jugular
Immediately reduces portosystemic pressure gradient below 12
Controls acute refractory variceal bleeding in over 90%
Resolves refractory cirrhotic ascites

right.title: TIPS Procedure Risks
points: Bypasses hepatic detoxification of ammonia and amines
Triggers or worsens hepatic encephalopathy in 30%
Stent stenosis or thrombosis requiring surveillance
Risk of liver capsular perforation during puncture

steps.tx: Acute thrombosis of the major hepatic veins or the retrohepatic IVC is designated **Budd-Chiari syndrome**. Impaired hepatic venous outflow provokes acute sinusoidal engorgement, ischemic hepatocyte necrosis, intractable painful hepatomegaly, and rapid-onset tense ascites, requiring emergent thrombolysis or TIPS to salvage hepatic parenchyma.
steps.say: Budd-Chiari syndrome results from thrombosis of the hepatic veins. Blocked outflow triggers hepatocyte necrosis, tender hepatomegaly, and tense ascites, requiring thrombolysis or TIPS.

rows: Sudden occlusion of all 3 major hepatic veins
Severe RUQ pain, jaundice, rapid tense ascites
TIPS decompression or orthotopic liver transplant
Toxic injury to microvascular terminal venules
Bone marrow transplant toxicity, jaundice, weight gain
